x: FFOnto is an ontology for forest-fire situational awareness. It turns drone images, field audio and fire-weather records into one knowledge graph that people and software can question, with every answer traceable to the record and the model it came from.

During a wildfire, evidence arrives in different forms. A drone frame shows smoke over a ridge, a microphone picks up a crackle or an explosion, and the weather station reports low humidity and a rising Fire Weather Index (FWI). Machine-learning models turn each of these into labels, captions and scores, but those outputs live in separate files, use different vocabularies and often disagree with each other. The Forest Fire Ontology (FFOnto) gives these sources one shared meaning. It defines what a fire event, a data record, a scene entity and a model observation are, and how they relate. Data described with FFOnto becomes a knowledge graph : a network of facts that can be queried with SPARQL, checked for consistency, and extended by rules that derive conditions, conflicts and hazards. Three ideas shape the ontology: World, data and claims are kept apart. When a classifier says smoke, 0.73 , FFOnto records that as a claim about an image, with its confidence, threshold and model, not as a fact about the fire. Conflicting claims can then sit side by side and be compared. Fine-grained kinds are a vocabulary, not a class hierarchy. Helmets, Pulaskis, crown fires and scorched trees are SKOS concepts. A new tool or hazard is one new concept, and the schema does not change. Knowledge that can be computed is derived by rules. Danger conditions, cross-modal conflicts and hazards are produced by SPARQL rules from the stored observations, so changing a threshold never means editing data.

FFOnto was developed in five stages. Each stage produced an artefact that the next one builds on, and evaluation results fed back into the earlier stages. The Development Lifecycle chapter describes each stage in detail. The five stages of the FFOnto development lifecycle, with feedback from evaluation Knowledge acquisition dataset, literature Requirements competency questions Implementation OWL, SKOS, rules, SHACL, JSON-LD Evaluation reasoner, ROBOT, OOPS!, CQ tests KG construction lifting, GraphDB, publication evaluation findings revise the questions and the model
This chapter follows FFOnto from the first look at the data to a validated knowledge graph. Each section corresponds to one stage of the lifecycle.

The starting point was the ForestFire-VQA dataset and the first version of FFOnto. The dataset combines drone images, field audio and fire-weather tables with more than a thousand question–answer pairs written about them. Reading those questions shows what people actually want to know: whether smoke is above a detection threshold, whether firefighters wear the right protective equipment, what the FWI trend is, and which hazards a scene contains. The first version of the ontology had grown without that focus. It contained duplicated concepts, classes that no question used, and properties that connected unrelated parts of the model. Model outputs were stored as if they were facts about the world, which made it impossible to represent two models disagreeing. The conceptual model for version 2 separates three layers: FFOnto layers: world, data and claims, and the relations between them World Data Claims FireEvent one fire incident Site station, camera, grid cell SceneEntity firefighter, fire front, house kind from the vocabulary ImageRecord AudioRecord WeatherRecord Caption SceneDescription output of a vision model ModelObservation class, confidence, threshold attributed to a Model Derived by rules detected class, condition ModalityConflict Hazard and actions about claims depicts Data records are about events and depict scene entities; model observations are claims about the records. The world layer holds what exists: fire events, sites and the entities seen in a scene. The data

Requirements were written as competency questions (CQs). Every question in ForestFire-VQA was mapped to the query pattern that would answer it, and questions that share a pattern were grouped. 1,004 dataset questions reduce to 27 competency questions . 291 of the dataset questions are general knowledge (for example, how to treat smoke inhalation) rather than questions about a specific record, so they are answered from documents rather than the knowledge graph. Group Competency questions Example dataset question Records and metadata CQ01–CQ03, CQ07b What is the image file checksum (SHA-256)? Model scores and captions CQ04–CQ07 Is the smoke score above the smoke threshold? Weather and FWI CQ08–CQ10 Is wind speed high enough to reduce aerial drop effectiveness? Scene content CQ11–CQ22 Are firefighters wearing helmets? Sound events CQ23 Is an explosion detected in the latest audio clip? Risk, response and ecology CQ24–CQ26 Are responders at risk from exploding materials? Two rules followed from this stage. A term enters the ontology only if a competency question needs it, and every competency question must be answerable by one tested SPARQL query.

The ontology is written in Turtle and split into modules, so the schema stays small while the vocabulary grows: Core schema ( ffonto-core.ttl ): 23 classes, 40 object properties and 57 datatype properties in OWL 2 DL. External terms from SOSA, PROV-O, SKOS and Dublin Core are declared locally, so the ontology loads offline. Vocabulary ( ffonto-vocab.ttl ): 374 SKOS concepts organised with skos:broader . Concepts carry keywords ( skos:hiddenLabel ) and background knowledge such as required PPE and the actions that mitigate a hazard. Danger rules ( danger-rules.ttl ): weather and FWI thresholds stored as data. Derivation rules R00–R08: SPARQL CONSTRUCT queries that derive detections, caption concepts, danger conditions, modality conflicts, hazards and the previous weather record. SHACL shapes for data quality, and a JSON-LD context that lifts the raw JSON and CSV files into RDF. ffonto:ModelObservation a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf sosa:Observation ; rdfs:label "Model observation"@en ; rdfs:comment "A claim made by a model about a data record: either a predicted class with a confidence (ffonto:predictedClass) or a categorical value for an observable property (sosa:observedProperty + ffonto:hasValueConcept)."@en . ffontov:Pulaski a skos:Concept ; skos:prefLabel "Pulaski"@en ; skos:inScheme ffontov:EntityKindScheme ; skos:broader ffontov:HandTool ; skos:hiddenLabel "pulaski"@en .

The ontology and the knowledge graph were checked at several levels: Check Tool Result OWL 2 DL profile ROBOT Passes Consistency of schema and data HermiT reasoner Consistent Negative tests (deliberately wrong data) HermiT 4 of 4 detected as inconsistent Labels, definitions, SKOS hygiene ROBOT report with a custom profile 0 errors, 0 warnings Modelling pitfalls OOPS! Remaining items reviewed and documented Every CQ answers correctly on test data pytest suite 59 tests pass Data quality of the lifted graph SHACL (pySHACL) Conforms The question-answering assistant built on the graph is evaluated separately, stage by stage: routing, choice of competency question, query execution, answer quality and faithfulness to the evidence. In preliminary runs on held-out ForestFire-VQA questions, routing between the knowledge graph and general knowledge reached 0.985 accuracy, and choosing the right competency question reached 0.767. The end-to-end evaluation is waiting for scene graphs extracted from all dataset images.

Raw records are lifted into RDF in four steps: Normalise. A Python lifter reads each image JSON, audio JSON and weather CSV row, fixes missing values and builds stable identifiers, for example one site per weather grid cell. Map. The JSON-LD context turns each field into an ontology term, so confidence becomes ffonto:confidence and event_id links the record to its ffonto:FireEvent . Load. The graph is stored in GraphDB in one repository with a named graph per source: ontology, vocabulary, image, audio, weather, scene and inferred. The RDFS-Plus ruleset adds subclass and inverse inferences. Derive. Rules R00–R08 run as SPARQL updates into the inferred graph, which is rebuilt on every load. The ontology itself is published as HTML documentation, with Turtle, RDF/XML and JSON-LD downloads, at the ontology documentation site .

FFOnto integrates three modalities. This chapter describes where each comes from, what a raw record looks like, and how its fields become ontology terms. All three are lifted the same way. A normaliser cleans the raw record, the JSON-LD context maps each field to an ontology term, and records that share an event_id are linked to the same ffonto:FireEvent . That shared event is what makes cross-modal questions possible, such as whether the audio and the image of one incident agree.

Weather records are rows of a table that combines daily weather observations with the components of the Canadian Fire Weather Index (FWI) system. Two public datasets provide the rows: Forest Fires (Montesinho natural park, Portugal). 517 records with a 9 × 9 spatial grid position, month and weekday, weather values, FWI components and the burned area (Cortez and Morais, 2007). The records carry no year or day of month, so they enter the graph without an observation date. Algerian Forest Fires (Bejaia and Sidi Bel-Abbès regions). Daily records from June to September 2012 with full dates, weather values, all six FWI components and a fire / no-fire class. Both are harmonised into one schema: modality,site,grid_x,grid_y,country,day_name,day_of_month,month_num,year,temp_c,rh_pct,wind_kmh,rain_mm,FFMC,DMC,DC,ISI,BUI,FWI,fire_occured,area_ha,event_id Tabular,demo_site_A,2,2,,tue,28,8,2012,17.4,43,6.7,0,94.8,108.3,647.1,17.0,150.4,33.1,1,1.07,ev_demo_081 Column Ontology term Meaning site , grid_x , grid_y ffonto:atSite → ffonto:Site One site per grid cell year , month_num , day_of_month ffonto:observationDate Only built when all three are present temp_c , rh_pct , wind_kmh , rain_mm ffonto:airTemperatureC , ffonto:relativeHumidityPct , ffonto:windSpeedKmh , ffonto:rainMm Daily weather FFMC , DMC , DC , ISI , BUI , FWI ffonto:ffmc … ffonto:fwi FWI system components fire_occured , area_ha ffonto:fireOccurred , ffonto:burnedAreaHa Outcome event_id ffonto:aboutEvent Links the row to a fir

Images are drone and camera frames from the ForestFire-VQA dataset. Each image has a JSON record produced by the image pipeline: a caption from an image-captioning model (BLIP, large); zero-shot scores for smoke , fire and no fire from CLIP ViT-L/14; the decision thresholds in use; file provenance and a SHA-256 checksum. { "record_uuid": "3f6d562f-33d3-49ee-a40b-3a8b6cf07823", "modality": "Image", "image_id": "evoDJI_0001_frame12_100788", "event_id": "ev_bf59c56acb36", "capture_time_utc": null, "labels": [ {"type": "fire", "confidence": 0.1585, "label_source": "caption", "model_name": "openai/clip-vit-large-patch14", "thresholds": {"fire_threshold": 0.55, "smoke_threshold": 0.6}}, {"type": "smoke", "confidence": 0.7291, "label_source": "zshot", "model_name": "openai/clip-vit-large-patch14"} ], "provenance": { "uri": "evoDJI_0001_frame12.jpg", "checksum_sha256": "df5124eb…", "caption_model": "Salesforce/blip-image-captioning-large", "caption_text": "arafed forest fire in the middle of a forest with a lake" }, "license": "CC-BY-4.0", "image_size_px": {"width": 2048, "height": 1080} } Field Becomes the record itself ffonto:ImageRecord each entry of labels an ffonto:ModelObservation with ffonto:predictedClass , ffonto:confidence and prov:wasAttributedTo the model thresholds ffonto:Threshold individuals, linked with ffonto:usedThreshold caption_text an ffonto:Caption ; rule R03 tags the concepts it mentions checksum_sha256 , uri , license , size record metadata ( ffonto:checksumSH

Audio clips are recorded at or near the fire. Each clip is classified with YAMNet, a sound-event model with 521 classes. YAMNet scores the clip in frames of 0.48 seconds, and the pipeline keeps the labels that reach a frame threshold of 0.2 and maps them to fire-relevant sound events: { "record_uuid": "7cd6773c-c37e-4acc-a594-20a8d0a5c74a", "modality": "Audio", "audio_file": "videoplayback_14.wav", "event_id": "ev_22e029d3b190", "duration_ms": 480.0, "labels": [ {"type": "fire_audio", "raw_label": "explosion", "mean_confidence": 0.7337, "max_confidence": 0.7337, "topk_frame_labels": ["explosion"], "thresholds": {"frame_thresh": 0.2}} ], "provenance": {"model": "https://tfhub.dev/google/yamnet/1", "frame_stride_s": 0.48, "thresh": 0.2, "topk": 8} } Field Becomes the record itself ffonto:AudioRecord with ffonto:durationMs raw_label ffonto:predictedClass pointing to a sound-event concept, for example ffontov:Explosion mean_confidence , max_confidence ffonto:meanConfidence , ffonto:maxConfidence model , frame_stride_s , topk model provenance ( ffonto:modelURL , ffonto:frameStrideS , ffonto:topK ) Audio matters most in combination. When an explosion is detected above its threshold, rule R07 derives an explosion hazard for the event. Independently, rule R06 derives the same hazard type when a propane tank is seen near the fire in an image of that event. Both hazards share the hazard type ffontov:ExplosionHazard , and the vocabulary supplies its recommended actions: cool and isolate

FFOnto-Bot is a chat assistant that answers questions in plain English from the FFOnto knowledge graph. It runs entirely on local models, and every answer shows the query and the facts it was based on. How FFOnto-Bot answers a question: routing to the knowledge graph, document search or a short reply Question + selected record Router local LLM Knowledge graph tested CQ query, or checked generated SPARQL Short reply greetings, help Documents ontology facts, text, tables and figures Answer + evidence + chart

The source code is at https://github.com/kosala0514/ffonto-bot . The repository contains: the ontology modules; the lifting scripts and the derivation rules; the 27 competency-question queries and their tests; the GraphDB loader; the assistant itself: the FastAPI service, the Streamlit chat interface, an optional MCP server and the evaluation scripts.

FFOnto-Bot needs GraphDB with the FFOnto repository loaded, and Ollama for the local language models. A GPU with 16 GB of memory runs the default 14-billion-parameter model comfortably. Get the models. ollama pull qwen2.5:14b # routing and answers ollama pull bge-m3 # embeddings for search ollama pull qwen2.5vl:7b # optional: reads figures in documents Install and index. pip install -r qa/requirements-qa.txt python graphdb/load_graphdb.py # load ontology, data and rules into GraphDB python -m qa.build_index # example questions and documents Start the service and the chat. uvicorn qa.api:app --port 8000 streamlit run qa/ui_streamlit.py # opens http://localhost:8501 Ask. Choose an image or audio record in the sidebar, then ask about it, for example Are the firefighters wearing gloves? , Is the smoke score above the threshold? or What hazards are present? . Questions about weather need a site and date, such as What was the FWI at Bejaia on 2012-06-07? . Open Evidence under an answer to see the query and rows.

Answers from the graph, not from memory For questions about data, the language model only chooses which tested competency-question query to run. The answer is written from the returned rows alone. If the graph has no evidence, the bot says so instead of guessing. Questions outside the 27 patterns When no competency question fits, the bot writes its own SPARQL from the ontology schema. The query is checked first: read-only, a row limit enforced, and only ontology terms used. It runs only if it passes. General wildfire knowledge Definitions and advice come from your own documents and the ontology's background knowledge, with citations. Charts, maps and tables inside PDFs are searchable too, and the figures an answer relies on are shown with it. Visual answers Results such as model scores against thresholds, FWI trends or weather against danger thresholds come with a chart drawn from the same rows. Traceable evidence Every reply carries its route, the competency question, the SPARQL query, the result rows and the sources. Private by design All models run locally through Ollama, so no data or question leaves the machine. Tool access for other agents An optional MCP server exposes the knowledge graph as tools: list and run competency questions, run SPARQL, look up ontology terms and search documents.

Fire and emergency analysts who need a quick, explainable summary of what the images, audio and weather say about an incident, including where they disagree. Researchers in knowledge graphs, multimodal learning and disaster informatics who want a tested benchmark for ontology-grounded question answering. Data and model developers who want to inspect model outputs, thresholds and provenance across a dataset. Educators and students learning about fire weather, firefighter safety and semantic technologies. FFOnto-Bot supports decisions and does not replace them. Model outputs can be wrong, the danger thresholds in version 2.0.0 are placeholders, and operational decisions remain with qualified personnel.
FFOnto data is queried with SPARQL. This chapter shows where to send queries and gives tested examples you can adapt.

A query needs the ontology, the vocabulary and the data in one place. There are three common ways to get that. In GraphDB Load the repository with the provided loader, then open the GraphDB Workbench at http://localhost:7200 , choose the ffonto repository and use the SPARQL editor. Each source is in its own named graph, so you can query everything or restrict a query to one modality: SELECT ?g (COUNT(*) AS ?triples) WHERE { GRAPH ?g { ?s ?p ?o } } GROUP BY ?g ORDER BY ?g # , …/audio, …/weather, …/scene, …/inferred, …/ontology, …/vocab Programs can use the same repository as a SPARQL endpoint: curl -s http://localhost:7200/repositories/ffonto \ -H "Accept: text/csv" \ --data-urlencode "query=PREFIX ffonto: SELECT (COUNT(?r) AS ?records) WHERE { ?r a ffonto:DataRecord }" In Python For small graphs, rdflib is enough. Load the ontology modules and the lifted data, then query: from rdflib import Graph g = Graph() for f in ["ontology/ffonto-core.ttl", "ontology/ffonto-vocab.ttl", "ontology/danger-rules.ttl", "data/kg_inferred.ttl"]: g.parse(f, format="turtle") for row in g.query(open("queries/CQ05.rq").read()): print(row.record, row["class"], row.confidence, row.threshold) data/kg_inferred.ttl already contains the facts derived by the rules. If you load the raw data/kg.ttl instead, run python scripts/run_cqs.py first, which applies the rules. Things to know Kinds are concepts. Ask for ?e ffonto:hasKind ffontov:Firefighter , not for a class ffonto:Firefighter . To include narrower k

OPTIONAL { ?o ffonto:aboveThreshold ?aboveThreshold } } ORDER BY ?record ?class On the example image from Data Sources , this returns fire 0.16, threshold 0.55, false and smoke 0.73, threshold 0.60, true . Where FFOnto can be used, what it cannot do yet, who helped build it, and how to cite it.

Incident situational awareness Combine what the drone images show, what the microphones hear and what the weather implies for one fire event, and see hazards with their recommended actions in one place. Firefighter safety checks Compare the protective equipment seen in an image with the equipment each role requires, and flag what is missing. Model monitoring Because model outputs are stored as observations with thresholds and provenance, the graph shows where classifiers, captioners and audio taggers disagree. These cases are useful for reviewing models and data. Fire-weather analysis Query FWI components and their trend by site and date, and see which operational conditions the danger rules imply. Explainable question answering FFOnto-Bot shows how an ontology can keep a language model's answers tied to evidence. It can serve as a baseline for research on knowledge-graph question answering. Post-fire assessment and teaching Burn evidence, ecosystem impacts and restoration measures in the vocabulary support damage assessment and teaching about fire ecology.

Limitation Planned work The danger-rule thresholds are placeholders. Replace them with values from published fire-danger classifications, each with its source. Scene facts are only as good as the vision-language model that extracts them. Measure extraction precision and recall on a hand-annotated subset, and keep human validation flags. Spatial relations such as near are judged from the image, not measured. Add geometry with GeoSPARQL where coordinates are available. Many records lack capture time and coordinates, which limits linking across modalities. Use the SHACL reports to complete metadata at capture time. Confidence of individual scene entities is not stored yet. Model scene attributes as observations with confidence, like classifier scores. The assistant answers each message on its own. Support follow-up questions in a conversation. The end-to-end evaluation of the assistant is preliminary. Evaluate on all held-out ForestFire-VQA questions once scene graphs exist for every image, and compare with a vision-language model answering directly from the image.

FFOnto was developed by Charuni Kosala Jayaweera under the supervision of Prof. Dulani Meedeniya. The work builds on open standards and tools: the W3C SOSA, PROV-O, SKOS and SHACL recommendations and DCMI Metadata Terms. It also builds on the ROBOT tool and the HermiT reasoner for validation, the OOPS! pitfall scanner, WIDOCO for the ontology documentation, GraphDB for storage, and Ollama with open Qwen models for the assistant. The weather data come from the public Forest Fires (Montesinho) and Algerian Forest Fires datasets in the UCI Machine Learning Repository.
